Module io.github.brantunger.unruly.core
Package io.github.brantunger.unruly.api.language

Interface EvaluationContext

All Known Subinterfaces:
ActionContext
public sealed interface EvaluationContext permits ActionContext (not exhaustive)
What a condition is evaluated against.

Implemented by the engine, which passes it to a language. It's sealed, so a language can't implement it; a language's unit tests create one with io.github.brantunger.unruly.test.LanguageTestContexts, from the unruly-engine-test artifact. Because only the engine implements it, a later release can add methods to it without breaking languages.

Identity: a context equals only itself, however its facts change and whatever another run's facts are, and its hashCode() reads neither the facts nor, for an ActionContext, the output object. A run passes one evaluation context to every condition, and a new action context to each action, so the two are different objects. A Session serves one run at a time and later runs reuse it, and no call to it marks where a run starts or ends, so state a run leaves in a session is still there for the next run; state for one run belongs in runScoped(java.lang.Object, java.util.function.Supplier<? extends T>), or, if it holds a resource that must be released, such as a runtime's context or interpreter opened for the run, in runScopedClosing(java.lang.Object, java.util.function.Supplier<? extends T>), which closes it when the run ends. A map keyed on contexts must not keep them alive, as a WeakHashMap doesn't.

    • facts

    • isCancelled

      boolean isCancelled()
      Returns whether the run must stop, because its thread has been interrupted or it has passed its deadline.

      The engine checks this itself before each condition and each action, and again when each one returns, so a language that evaluates an expression and returns needn't. A language whose expressions can stop part-way polls it, or maps it to its own cancellation, so a long-running expression stops too. Returning any value is enough: the engine stops the run as soon as the expression returns, whatever it returned. Throwing an exception once the run is cancelled stops the run the same way; an Error, or an exception with one anywhere in its cause chain, such as one wrapping what a fact's Java code threw, is still that rule's failure. A language that can't stop inside an expression runs it to its end, and the run stops when it returns.

      Returns:
      true if the run must stop

    • deadline

      @Nullable Instant deadline()
      Returns when the run must stop, from the timeout its engine or its run call was given: when the run started, on the system clock, plus its timeout. So it compares with Instant.now(), and shows the deadline a person or a log expects.

      It is for showing. What stops the run is measured with a monotonic clock from when the run started, so a step of the system clock while the run goes on moves Instant.now(), but not when the run stops. To time a language's own work, use timeLeft(), which is exact; isCancelled() says whether the run must stop.

      Returns:
      The deadline, or null if the run has none

    • timeLeft

      default Duration timeLeft()
      Returns how long the run has left before it must stop, measured as the engine measures it. A language that gives a call of its own a timeout, such as a script it runs on another thread, gives it this much time; working it out from deadline() and Instant.now() instead is off by as much as the system clock has been stepped since the run started.

      A run without a deadline has Duration.ofNanos(Long.MAX_VALUE), about 292 years, and a run whose deadline is further away than that has a little less: so the time left always converts with Duration.toNanos() or Duration.toMillis() without overflowing. The time left says nothing about an interrupt: isCancelled() answers for both.

      Returns:
      The time left: positive while the deadline is ahead, Duration.ZERO once it has passed, and at most Duration.ofNanos(Long.MAX_VALUE)

    • runScoped

      default <T> T runScoped(Object key, Supplier<? extends T> init)
      Returns the value kept under key for this run, making it with init the first time any condition or action of the run asks for it. So a language that converts the facts before it evaluates an expression, such as with FactProperties.toData(java.lang.Object, int), can convert them once per run rather than once per expression.

      Every condition and action of one run() shares the values: the evaluation context and each action context of the run return the same value for a key. A nested run has values of its own, and the next run starts with none. A key the language owns, such as its compiler, keeps its values apart from another language's. The same key must always hold the same type, or the caller gets a ClassCastException.

      The value is made when it is first asked for, and isn't made again during the run, so it doesn't see a change that Java code makes to a fact later in the run. The engine keeps the values until the run returns, and then lets them go without closing them: a resource a language opens for one run belongs in runScopedClosing(java.lang.Object, java.util.function.Supplier<? extends T>), which closes it when the run ends, and one it keeps from run to run in its Session. The values aren't synchronized, as a run evaluates one expression at a time. If init throws, nothing is kept, and the next call for the key calls its init again. An init can ask for other keys, but not for its own: that throws IllegalStateException, rather than recursing or making the value twice.

      Type Parameters:
      T - The value's type
      Parameters:
      key - The key, compared with Object.equals(Object)
      init - Makes the value the first time the run asks for key
      Returns:
      The value kept under key, never null
      Throws:
      NullPointerException - if key or init is null, or init returns null
      IllegalStateException - if the init of key is running, so it asked for its own key, or the run keeps a value under key with runScopedClosing(java.lang.Object, java.util.function.Supplier<? extends T>)

    • runScopedClosing

      default <T extends AutoCloseable> T runScopedClosing(Object key, Supplier<? extends T> init)
      Returns the value kept under key for this run, as runScoped(java.lang.Object, java.util.function.Supplier<? extends T>) does, and closes it when the run ends. It is for a resource a language opens for one run and must release, such as a runtime's context or interpreter, or a connection the run's expressions share.

      The engine closes the values once the run has ended, however it ends: it returns, fails, passes its deadline or is interrupted. It closes them on the thread that ran it, after the run's last listener call and before run() returns. The run still holds its copy of the rules then, so no other run uses its sessions until its values are closed, and no session of the copy is closed before them. They are closed in the reverse of the order they were made, so a value whose init asked for another is closed before that one, and each is closed whatever the others throw. What a close() throws is handled as what a Session.close() throws is: it is logged at WARN, and the run's outcome stands, unless it is a fatal Error, such as an OutOfMemoryError. Once every value is closed, run() throws that error in place of the result, or of a failure of the run that isn't fatal, which the error carries as a suppressed exception; a run that failed with a fatal error of its own throws its own, carrying the one from close(). A nested run closes its own values when it ends.

      A key is either closing or not: asking with this method for a key that the run keeps a value under with runScoped(java.lang.Object, java.util.function.Supplier<? extends T>), or the other way round, throws IllegalStateException. So does asking for a value with this method once the run's values are being closed, or have been, such as from a value's close() or through a context kept past its run, as that value would never be closed. Unlike runScoped(java.lang.Object, java.util.function.Supplier<? extends T>), this method can be called from another thread while the run ends: the value is then either closed with the run's others, or refused with IllegalStateException, and never left open. A language's unit tests close a test context's values with io.github.brantunger.unruly.test.LanguageTestContexts.endRun. Otherwise the values behave as runScoped(java.lang.Object, java.util.function.Supplier<? extends T>) describes.

      Type Parameters:
      T - The value's type
      Parameters:
      key - The key, compared with Object.equals(Object)
      init - Makes the value the first time the run asks for key
      Returns:
      The value kept under key, never null
      Throws:
      NullPointerException - if key or init is null, or init returns null
      IllegalStateException - if the init of key is running, so it asked for its own key, the run keeps a value under key with runScoped(java.lang.Object, java.util.function.Supplier<? extends T>), or the run's values are being or have been closed
